prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B001 prize to Holst, Drucker and Mojsov. Round 1 showed that all six of us reach it on the same merit argument and not only from the opening tally: proglucagon processing and the active GLP-1(7-36) amide, human incretin physiology, then receptor-based therapies with large randomized outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism is understood end to end and independently confirmed over two decades, and clinical reach is unmatched on the shortlist. Because the same three names and the same single-part form appear in every file, I use this round to test the credit and not to restate the headline. The test did not move me. The citation names the physiology and the active form, and the verb made possible links it to the drugs without claiming that these three laureates made them. I keep one achievement because a second part would split three places and weaken both parts.
statement.case_against: The weakness remains attribution, and I do not want unanimity to hide it. Lotte Bjerre Knudsen's acylation chemistry is what turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-weekly drug, so the citation honours the hormone and its discovery more directly than the medicines. Mojsov's priority against Joel Habener's group is still something none of us has settled from the supplied records. Each of us has said we rely on general knowledge, and I count myself in that. If the committee cannot defend naming Mojsov on documents it can cite, the credit would need to change, and the fallback of Holst, Drucker and Knudsen is a substantive change in what the prize honours, not a swap of one name.

responses.point: Sandberg places Knudsen on the drug-design side of the line and, in the same file, treats Mojsov's contribution as decisive yet contested. He keeps the discovery trio because the long-acting analogues depend on the physiology.
responses.response: I agree with the outcome and have not moved. I would not rest it on the word industrial, though. The test I apply is whether the citation can truthfully say what these three people did, and made possible does that for the physiology and the active peptide. Your contested remark about Mojsov is the part I take most seriously. I cannot resolve it from the supplied files, and I do not think we should vote as if we had. My position is to name her on the strength of the identification and synthesis of the active form, while saying openly that this rests on my general knowledge. If the committee found that record unsupported, I would reopen the third name before moving the headline.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius says engineering a native peptide into a once-weekly drug is a scientific achievement and not routine development. She is open to replacing one of the three, and Mojsov is where she would hesitate most.
responses.response: I accept your correction that Knudsen's work is science and not routine development, and it sharpens my own case against. We still differ on what follows. If Knudsen replaced Mojsov, the prize would honour the hormone's physiology (Holst, Drucker) and the drug chemistry, but would no longer credit identification of the active peptide, which the drug-development arm also relies on. That is a different citation and I would want it argued as such. Replacing Holst or Drucker is harder still, because human incretin physiology and receptor biology are the core. So I would hold the discovery trio unless the Mojsov record fails. At that point the Holst-Drucker-Knudsen option that El-Manira described becomes the principled fallback, and I would support it.

responses.point: El-Manira names Holst-Drucker-Knudsen, or a narrower physiology citation, as the fallback if Mojsov's priority is judged too unclear, and calls that a substantive change. She or he also keeps optogenetics (B012) as a strong alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the fallback is a different prize and not a detail, and I accept it as the right contingency. On B012 I have not changed my mind from round 1. I share your view that it is Nobel-scale, but nothing in the discussion has produced a rule for cutting six names to three. Linnarsson and Sandberg both noted that each omitted contributor, Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenboeck, carries a decisive step. I would not name B012 as an alternative to B001 that I could defend, so I keep it off my alternatives list. I would take it up again only if the committee agreed on how to separate channel discovery from neuronal deployment.

responses.point: Linnarsson keeps a single-achievement prize, because a second part would force a split of the laureate slots that dilutes both. He treats Eshhar's early receptor work as an open question for B017.
responses.response: I agree on the single-achievement form, and Perlmann made the same point about shrinking each of the three GLP-1 credits. On Eshhar and B017 I am less certain than I was. Rosenberg's best case is adoptive transfer and early engineered-T-cell trials, not CAR design, so a June-Sadelain-Rosenberg trio does not map onto a single clean discovery. I still count B017 as my first alternative because the clinical evidence is strong and it is a new modality. I would want the committee to settle the Rosenberg and Eshhar question explicitly before it relies on B017, because it is not yet as defensible as B001.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide relative to Habener's group can be stated from documents the committee can cite. I have not verified it and still rely on general knowledge.
Whether the citation should be physiology-led, as I propose, or whether Knudsen should enter if the Mojsov record fails. In that case I would favour Holst, Drucker and Knudsen.
For B017, the correct credit for Rosenberg and Eshhar, which would decide whether it is a defensible second choice.
For B004, whether Druker, Lydon and Sawyers can be framed as a self-contained therapeutic achievement when Rowley, Nowell, Baltimore and others fall outside the credit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the preferred configuration or the alternatives. I disclose frequent co-authorship with Thomas Perlmann on dopamine-neuron work and training with Paul Greengard. Neither is connected to any shortlisted candidate, and I know of no personal tie to any credited name. No other member's round-1 disclosure changes this.
